title: Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings
one_liner: Remove the half-day minimum by dispatching remote stenographers into many short hearings per day, so a family-law litigant gets a certified record of a 15-minute hearing for about $100.
customer: California family law and probate attorneys and solo practitioners. Self-represented litigants reached through DV legal aid organizations and family law facilitators. Legal aid groups buying bulk credits. Later, county courts contracting to meet the new duty to provide records to indigent litigants.
problem: California logged roughly 3 million civil, family and probate hearings without a verbatim record between April 2023 and March 2026, about 7 in 10. Without a record, appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail, because the appellant cannot show error. Private reporters charge $250-$500+ appearance minimums, since a reporter can wait 2-3 hours for a 12-minute calendar item. Nobody pays that for a routine hearing. In 2026 the California Supreme Court (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) held that courts must give indigent litigants an official verbatim record on request, and courts do not have the reporters to comply.
solution: A dispatch platform that reads court calendars, predicts when each matter will be called from historical hearing-type durations per department, and pages a remote reporter into the court's Zoom or Teams feed only for the minutes needed. One reporter covers 8-12 short hearings a day across departments. Deliver a certified transcript in 24-72 hours, with an AI first draft for the reporter to scope. Price is a flat $95 for hearings up to 15 minutes and about $8 per page beyond that. Start where remote appearance and remote reporting are allowed (California's AB 3013 authorizes remote reporting, and each court's procedures need checking). Pitch courts on per-department-day capacity at a discount to staffing a full-time reporter.
why_now: The 2026 California Supreme Court ruling creates a legal duty courts cannot currently meet. AB 3013 (2024) opened remote reporting. The workforce is projected to be about 5,500 reporters short by 2030. Family courts are widely on video. Reporter dead time is a scheduling problem that software can solve.
revenue_model: Per-hearing fees paid by attorneys and litigants. Bulk credits funded by legal aid and foundation grants. Later B2G contracts priced per courtroom-day. The reporter keeps about 55-60% of each hearing fee, which beats their typical hourly yield because dead time is eliminated.
non_obvious_insight: The reporter shortage is partly a utilization problem. In a busy family calendar department, a reporter may write 2-3 hours of a 7-hour day and wait the rest. Remote hopping sells that dead time to several litigants at once, so the price can fall 70% while the reporter earns more.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 remote-capable freelance or semi-retired reporters. Pick one county whose family departments run on Zoom and cover it manually with a shared spreadsheet and a text pager. Offer 10 solo family law attorneys and two DV appellate nonprofits (start with the Family Violence Appellate Project) at-cost coverage of their next 5 hearings. Track wait time per hearing so the prediction model has real data.

title: Retraining-Backed Severance for AI Layoffs
one_liner: Employers replace resume-coaching outplacement with prepaid seats in shortage-role training plus a guaranteed interview pipeline, priced per re-employed worker.
customer: HR and people-ops leaders at 500-20,000 person employers doing AI-related restructuring; hiring employers in healthcare and trades pay placement fees.
problem: Employment of 22-25 year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below trend and recent grads are 42% underemployed. About half the earnings loss comes from landing in restaurants and retail. Traditional outplacement coaches people back toward the same shrinking roles.
solution: Displaced workers choose from vetted 8-16 week programs into shortage jobs (medical assistant, EMT, CDL, electrician pre-apprenticeship, revenue-cycle, dental support). The employer funds tuition and a stipend from severance budget. Hiring partners guarantee interviews. Use Workforce Pell where a program is approved. Success fee at 90-day retention.
why_now: AI-linked layoffs are drawing PR and political pressure. Workforce Pell has only 5 approved programs, so employer-funded pathways are the fast lane. Employers in experience-rated unemployment-insurance states may also gain from faster re-employment (verify by state).
revenue_model: $4-9k per participant paid by the employer, replacing a $3-5k outplacement fee, plus $1-3k placement fees from hiring partners.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume laid-off white-collar workers should look for adjacent white-collar roles. Those roles are the ones disappearing. Severance is already budgeted money, so converting a slice into a retraining voucher aimed at shortage roles costs the employer little and buys reputation.
first_30_days: Build 3 vetted pathways with local providers in one metro. Pitch 20 HR heads at companies that recently announced cuts. Run a single 25-person pilot and collect 90-day placement outcomes for references.

title: Waste-Fat Origin Passports for 45Z Fuel
one_liner: Collector-level audits, chain of custody and lab fingerprinting that prove a load of used cooking oil or animal fat is North American.
customer: Renewable diesel, SAF and biodiesel producers, feedstock traders, and UCO collectors who want a price premium for proven origin.
problem: Since 2026, the 45Z clean-fuel credit has been limited to North American feedstocks, which creates an incentive to relabel imported UCO as domestic. Existing testing labs certify samples, not the collection chain, and producers face audit and credit-clawback risk.
solution: An 'origin passport' per load: KYC and site audits of collectors, GPS-tagged pickups, retained samples, and lab fingerprinting (fatty-acid and sterol profile, stable isotopes) against a growing reference library, delivered as per-load certificates and a traceability dashboard.
why_now: The 45Z origin restriction took effect for fuel made after 2025, so proof of origin has become a price factor. A UCO import surge and past fraud scandals mean auditors will look hard.
revenue_model: Per-load certificate fee of a few cents per gallon, annual collector audit fee, and subscription for producers.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is a fraud-prone commodity because the seller controls the paperwork. Verifying the collection chain, not the oil, is where enforcement will go.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 mid-size collectors and one independent biodiesel producer as design partners. Build a reference sample library from those partners. Set up a lab partnership. Run first 20 loads with passports.

title: Audit Desk for Indie Labels' AI-Remix Royalties
one_liner: Independent monitoring, consent management and statement auditing for the royalties that AI covers and remixes will start generating.
customer: Indie labels and publishers with 500-50,000 tracks, including Merlin, A2IM and IMPALA members, and their managers. Later, Merlin itself or collecting societies.
problem: Spotify and UMG will sell fan AI covers and remixes as a paid Premium add-on with 'consent, credit, compensation,' but no attribution method has been disclosed. Merlin joined on Aug 4, and Deezer's remix feature needs artist consent (Jun 24). Indie rights-holders will soon receive statement lines for derivative uses they cannot verify, across several programs with different opt-in rules.
solution: A dashboard that normalizes consent and pricing terms across programs (Spotify, Deezer, YouTube, licensed generators). An independent detector samples public remix and cover outputs using stem-level audio similarity to estimate each catalog's derivative usage. It reconciles the estimate against reported statements and prepares audit-rights letters when the numbers do not match. Delivered as a monthly report plus software.
why_now: The first major licensed-derivative programs launched in 2026, and Suno's Sep 9 move to a licensed-trained model shows a pay-for-use market forming. Indies have the least data and the weakest audit position.
revenue_model: $500-2,000/month per label, plus a contingency of 10-15% on recovered underpayments, which is standard for royalty audits, and an enterprise deal with an indie body.
non_obvious_insight: When a new royalty stream launches without a disclosed attribution method, the party with the least data needs an independent auditor. Royalty auditing is an established, profitable profession that no one has built for AI derivatives yet.
first_30_days: Take 10 indie labels through Merlin and A2IM contacts. Produce a free 'Derivative Exposure Report' scanning YouTube, TikTok and Deezer previews for AI covers of each label's top 50 tracks. Sell the monthly monitor, and recruit an advisor from a royalty-audit firm.

title: Independent Gauntlet for Police and Counter-Drone Buyers
one_liner: A buyer-funded, video-first test lab that flies and publishes open-protocol results on police first-responder drones and counter-drone detection, the way the Pentagon's public Gauntlets do for its own buyers, funded by agency subscriptions and never by vendors.
customer: Police, fire and emergency-management tech buyers at city and county agencies ($1,200-3,000 per agency-year for full data, vendor scorecards and RFP language), buyer consortia, and grant-funded counter-UAS programs (FEMA's $500M program, Dallas's $10M set-aside).
problem: Local buyers cannot audit vendors: state and local tech contracts average 7 years, only 5.3% of AI-relevant provisions address transparency, and GenAI-written RFPs make every proposal look perfect. Vendor claims are unreliable: only 24% of drones reached 10 km in the Pentagon's Gauntlet 1, Cape Canaveral's radars miss quadcopters, and 700+ drones were seized around one World Cup stadium. Trade media and cooperative marketplaces are vendor-funded, so independent performance data does not exist.
solution: Quarterly standardized tests covering range, wind, latency, false alarms against birds and RF clutter, and detection of cooperative test drones only (no jamming). Runs are recorded with signed telemetry and raw video so results cannot be disputed or edited, and protocols are open. Drone creators co-host as pilots and distribute the long-form video, while agencies pay for data, scorecards, sample RFP language and an ask-us desk. Vendors may buy re-tests only after results are public.
why_now: The Pentagon's public Gauntlets (Gauntlet 2 in Sept 2026: 23 platforms, 19 companies, 1,858 sorties) normalized head-to-head public testing. Counter-drone money is flowing to cities, sponsored and AI-written content swamps review media, and local surveillance-tech purchases now face public scrutiny.
revenue_model: Agency subscriptions, custom pre-procurement tests paid from grants, and paid training. No vendor sponsorship, which is the trust asset.
non_obvious_insight: DoD's Gauntlet works because the buyer controls the test. Local agencies have the same need but no lab budget, and the creator-media model (audience-funded, no sponsors) is exactly the structure that makes an independent lab self-sustaining. Vendor-funded trade media and vendor-listing marketplaces are structurally unable to be the referee.
first_30_days: Buy five sub-$5K first-responder-class drones and run one head-to-head on range, wind and latency, then publish it. Email 200 police tech sergeants and drone-as-first-responder coordinators and sign 10 agency subscriptions at $1,200. File public-records requests for existing agency test data to seed the second episode.

title: Grandschools: Microschools Inside Senior Communities
one_liner: Turnkey K-8 microschools hosted in senior-living and 55+ communities, with residents as mentors and tuition funded by ESAs and scholarship credits.
customer: Senior-living operators and 55+ communities (pay a program fee for engagement and occupancy marketing); families paying tuition, ESA or scholarship dollars; retired professionals as mentors.
problem: More than 1,000 public schools closed in 2025-26, families are being displaced, and microschools struggle to find trusted adults (at Alpha School two-thirds of guides lack teaching credentials). Senior communities struggle with purpose-driven programming and occupancy. Each side has the resource the other lacks.
solution: A franchise-lite pilot model of 12-24 kids, 1 lead guide and 6-10 resident 'grand-mentors' (retired engineers, teachers, nurses) running project blocks, sharing dining, garden and library space. A standard playbook covers background checks, safeguarding, insurance, private-school registration and a mentor-hour ledger. Enrollment through ESA and SGO scholarships.
why_now: The demographic cliff in kids meets the aging peak. Scholarship credits and ESAs from 2027 make tuition viable for middle-income families, and the microschool guide shortage is acute.
revenue_model: $6-9k per child in tuition or ESA funds; operator program fee of $1-2k a month (or free space); licensing and playbook fees when replicating.
non_obvious_insight: The two halves of the demographic shift are each other's missing input: shrinking youth cohorts leave surplus buildings, growing elderly cohorts hold surplus expertise, and aging-services operators have engagement budgets that schools have never tapped.
first_30_days: Approach 10 independent-living communities in one metro that have on-site classrooms and sign one. Recruit 10 families from closed-school parent groups and a certified guide. Launch a 'Fridays' pilot before a full schedule. Confirm state private-school registration and insurance first.

title: Open-Banking Rails for EU Connected Products
one_liner: A consent-and-access hub that lets manufacturers meet the EU Data Act's access-by-design duty and lets owners route product data to repairers, insurers and energy optimizers through one integration.
customer: Two sides. Forced buyers are manufacturers, importers and white-labelers of connected products sold in the EU (e-bikes, heat pumps, wallboxes, appliances, machinery, agricultural kit, wearables), paying per product family per year. The network side is independent repair chains, insurers, energy retailers, lenders and fleet managers paying per authorized device pull.
problem: Since 12 Sept 2026, connected products newly placed on the EU market must give users free, structured, machine-readable access to their data and share it with third parties on request. Most SME makers and importers have cloud endpoints never designed for this: no consent flow, no standard API, no logging, no trade-secret safeguards, no pre-sale disclosures. Third parties who want the data face hundreds of separate negotiations.
solution: A hosted 'Data Act portal' for the manufacturer covering ownership binding (QR or serial on the product), machine-readable export, consent to share with a named third party, trade-secret safeguards, access logs, a dispute workflow and the Art. 3(2) pre-contract disclosure templates. A normalized schema catalog per product category (for example 'heat pump v1') means third parties integrate once. We sell it first as a 90-day compliance kit, then monetize the network.
why_now: The access-by-design duty took effect 12 Sept 2026 and law-firm alerts show many makers unfinished. From 12 Jan 2027 cloud switching fees vanish, which makes data mobility a political priority. The regulation mandates giving data but says nothing about how anyone receives it.
revenue_model: Compliance SaaS at roughly EUR 300-3,000/month per product family. Network fees of EUR 0.02-0.50 per device per month from third-party consumers of the data. An optional certification badge for makers.
non_obvious_insight: The Data Act is open banking for machines, but with no PSD2-style standardization mandate: it creates a duty to give data with no way to receive it. Whoever standardizes the receiving side becomes the Plaid of physical products. The manufacturers, who are forced buyers today, pay for the network build.
first_30_days: Pick one fragmented vertical (e-bikes, or heat pumps and wallboxes). Publish a free 'is my product in scope' checker and a readiness checklist to generate leads. Sign 5 SME makers or importers to EUR 2k pilots that deliver a working access endpoint. Pitch two independent repair, insurance or energy firms as first consumers on the receiving side.

title: Listing Bodyguard: Scam-Listing Takedown for Property Managers
one_liner: Continuously scans the web for scam copies of a property manager's listings and takes them down, and gives real prospects a fast way to verify that a listing is legitimate.
customer: Property managers and leasing companies with 100 to 3,000 units, paying a monthly subscription. The buyer is the marketing or leasing director. Secondary buyers are apartment associations, large landlords' insurers and rental listing portals.
problem: Scammers copy a manager's real listing photos, undercut the rent by 25 to 40% and collect application fees and deposits from victims who never see the unit. Victims then show up at the property or call the leasing office furious, and often leave one-star reviews of the real manager. Real leads are poached by the fake listing, and the leasing team wastes hours on angry callers and manual takedown requests to Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace and others. There is no owner of the problem: the listing platforms are slow, police shrug and the PM's syndication vendor does not monitor. AI now makes it trivial to generate thousands of fake listings, with photos rewritten and descriptions localized.
solution: Pull each PM's live listing feed (from the syndication export in AppFolio, Buildium, Yardi or RentManager), compute perceptual hashes of every photo and fingerprints of the description text and address, then continuously search for matches across Craigslist, Zillow-family sites, Facebook (through allowed methods and user reports), OfferUp and the open web through reverse-image APIs. When a match appears on a listing whose contact does not belong to the PM, the system files takedown requests through each platform's copyright, fraud or impersonation channel with evidence, tracks status, and escalates. Prevention layer: every real listing gets a short verification code ('Verify: text 4471 to our verified line'), and a landing page confirms the unit and the real contact, giving prospects a free way to check before wiring money. Weekly reports show scams blocked, leads protected and estimated victim exposure.
why_now: Generative AI made scam listings cheap and scalable in 2025 and 2026, and consumer-protection agencies continue to list rental scams among the top fraud categories. Rental portals are under pressure to verify but are slow. The reverse-image and vision APIs from major providers make similarity search inexpensive, and the takedown channels are already documented, so a small team can automate a job that leasing staff currently do by hand.
revenue_model: $0.50 to $1.50 per active listing per month with a $199 monthly minimum, or a flat tier for portfolios. Upsell: white-label verification pages and analytics for apartment associations, and API licensing to listing portals and insurers who want fewer fraud claims.
non_obvious_insight: To a leasing office, a scam listing is not a consumer-fraud story. It is a top-of-funnel leak and a brand problem, because the scammer steals real leads and the victims blame the PM. Managers already know this but treat it as a nuisance, so there is a budget for a fix but no product. The real moat is the takedown playbook per platform: which channel, which wording, which contact person actually gets a listing removed within hours rather than days.
first_30_days: Manually audit 3 to 5 friendly PMs: take their public listings, run reverse-image searches and show them the scam copies already live (there will be some). That audit is the sales pitch, and most PMs have never looked. Build a script using Google Vision web-detection or TinEye plus Craigslist and Marketplace searches for a first pass, and a shared dashboard for takedown status. Charge $199 per month per portfolio starting in month 2. Ask each PM for a testimonial and a 'stopped 14 scams last quarter' number to bring to the next landlord association talk.

title: Rain-Day Revenue Insurance for Patio Restaurants
one_liner: Parametric weather cover for restaurants: pick your bad-weather trigger, get paid automatically when it hits, with payouts calibrated to your own POS history.
customer: Independent restaurants and bars with 1-10 units and meaningful patio or walk-up dependence, starting in weather-volatile metros (rain, extreme heat, wildfire smoke). The owner pays a seasonal premium of roughly $40-150 per location per month. A licensed MGA/carrier partner and reinsurer sit behind the product.
problem: A rainy Friday, a 105F heat-index evening or a smoke day (AQI over 150) can cut a patio-dependent night by 30-50%. The food is already prepped and the staff are already scheduled, so almost all of the lost revenue is lost margin. Business-interruption insurance needs physical damage, so weather-driven demand loss is uninsured. Every owner knows their 'rain tax' (I know a wet Saturday costs me several thousand dollars), yet no one sells a hedge for it.
solution: Owners connect Toast, Square or Clover, and we ingest 12-24 months of hourly sales. We fit each location's loss curve against local weather-station history, for example rain over 0.15 in between 5 and 9pm Fri-Sun, or heat index above 105. The owner picks triggers and a fixed payout per trigger day. When the station data crosses the threshold, the payout goes out automatically by instant rails, with no claim and no adjuster. Because triggers are calibrated per restaurant, basis risk is low, which is what has kept carriers away from this segment. We sell it as a seasonal policy with a monthly premium.
why_now: POS APIs now give clean hourly sales for thousands of independents in minutes. Weather-station and air-quality data are cheap and auditable. Instant payment rails (FedNow, RTP) exist. Heat domes and smoke seasons are making weather volatility a top-3 owner complaint. Reinsurers are hungry for parametric programs, and restaurants face rising conventional premiums that push them to look for smarter cover. I could not re-verify current competitors this session, so check the existing parametric MGAs and event-cancellation carriers before building.
revenue_model: MGA commission plus underwriting margin on premium, typically 15-30% of premium retained as fee and MGA share. Roughly $500-1,800 per location per year in premium. Add a fee for the POS-calibrated loss-curve analytics, sold to carriers and reinsurers as a data product.
non_obvious_insight: The trick is that the owner's POS data, not a claims adjuster, is the underwriting. Basis risk is what kills parametric for small businesses, and a restaurant's own hourly sales history fixes it. Insurers think restaurants are too heterogeneous to price. They are only heterogeneous until you fit each one separately. The loss is also asymmetric: prepped food and committed labor mean a payout only has to cover the lost contribution margin, not the revenue, so premiums can be low.
first_30_days: Use my two locations' POS exports plus 10 friendly patio owners' data to fit loss curves and prove the weather-to-sales correlation. Publish a free 'Rain Tax Report' for one metro to generate leads. Sign a licensed MGA or fronting-carrier partner. Collect 10-15 signed letters of intent at about $60 per month for the next patio season. Since it is late September, use the off-season to finish modeling and pre-sell spring renewals.

title: Facility-Clearance-in-a-Box and Cleared Bench
one_liner: A facility-clearance sponsor plus a rentable bench of already-cleared engineers for the wave of newly funded defense startups winning first classified subcontracts.
customer: Series A-C defense startups and small business subcontractors with a first classified task order but no facility clearance or cleared staff.
problem: Defense startups raised $14.6B in five months of 2026, and awards are accelerating. Startups cannot sponsor clearances without a contract and cannot start work without cleared people. Sponsorship and adjudication take months, so classified work stalls and startups lose the window.
solution: A cleared small business holds the FCL and employs a bench of cleared engineers, program managers and security officers. It subcontracts them to startups by the hour, provides FSO services, and manages the startup's own path to clearance. Includes shared SCIF time at partner facilities.
why_now: Record capital plus fast-lane vehicles (Megatron IDIQ, the Space Force valley-of-death office, Navy marketplaces) create hundreds of first-time classified subcontractors at once. Federal staff shortages mean primes want ready capacity.
revenue_model: Cleared-labor margin (25-40% on $150-250 per hour), monthly FSO retainers ($4-10K), and SCIF seat fees. A roll-up of small cleared staffing shops adds scale.
non_obvious_insight: Cash is no longer scarce for defense startups, but time-to-cleared-work is. The binding constraint has moved from funding to a slow, government-controlled credential that can be rented.
first_30_days: Acquire or partner with a small cleared firm that already holds an FCL. Recruit 5-8 cleared freelancers and retired government staff. Pitch the 20 most recently funded startups and place the first two engineers.

title: Contingency-Fee Meter Audits for Water Utilities
one_liner: Test the big commercial and industrial meters that under-register, replace them, and take a share of the new billed revenue for two years.
customer: Mid-size water and wastewater utilities (20k-500k connections) with large commercial bases, private regulated water companies, and utilities serving new large loads such as data centers and fabs. The utility pays from recovered revenue.
problem: Everyone sells AI leak detection, but in many audits apparent losses (meter under-registration, billing errors, unauthorized use) are comparable to real losses. Large compound meters under-register at low flow, and 1% of a data center's consumption is a lot of money. Utilities under rate pressure and drought-reduced volumes have no capex budget for meter programs.
solution: Prioritize the top 5% of accounts using billing anomalies (size versus consumption history). Field-test meters with a mobile test bench and clamp-on verification, then repair or replace. The company fronts the work and takes 20-35% of incremental revenue for 24 months. Software ranks accounts, and reports feed the AWWA-style utility audit.
why_now: Drought cuts volumes and rate pressure is intense. Private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 and must justify revenue. New industrial loads make each meter worth more.
revenue_model: 20-35% of incremental billed revenue for two years, with no upfront cost to the utility.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders chase leaks, which need capital and crews. Meter recovery is immediate cash with no capex approval, so it is easy to say yes to. Private and special-district utilities can sign contingency deals without a full municipal procurement.
first_30_days: Target three investor-owned utilities and two special districts. Offer a free desktop analysis of their top 200 commercial accounts using billing data. Test the ten most suspicious meters as a proof-of-value, and sign a contingency contract on the results.

title: Hospital Back-Office Campuses Become Staff Housing
one_liner: Help nonprofit health systems convert surplus administrative office campuses, emptied by AI scribes and revenue-cycle automation, into staff housing, with the hospital itself as the master-lease credit that makes the conversion financeable.
customer: Nonprofit health-system CFOs and real-estate heads pay a fixed-fee feasibility engagement plus a success fee. Development and lending partners are secondary.
problem: Health systems own large billing, coding and admin campuses just as ambient AI (over 70% of large delivery networks have deployed or piloted scribes) and revenue-cycle automation shrink back-office headcount. Medicaid work requirements threaten 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hits, and replacing a bedside nurse costs roughly $55-60K by industry surveys. Meanwhile office-conversion lenders will not fund without a credit tenant, and 2026 rates are punishing.
solution: A 'space-to-housing' package: a utilization audit of admin real estate (badge, Wi-Fi and parking data), floor-by-floor conversion screening, a 10-15 year staff-housing master lease structured as a recruiting and retention benefit (rent by payroll deduction), tax-exempt or community-benefit financing, and a co-development partner. Fee at financial close.
why_now: AI scribes and RCM automation went mainstream in 2025-26, and Medicaid cuts force hospitals to monetize idle assets. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months. Public-partnered conversions such as 100 Gold Street (4,000 units) show a mission-aligned pipeline. PE physician-practice deals are down about 50%, so systems are holding more real estate.
revenue_model: $40-90K feasibility fee, a 1-2% success fee or development-fee share at close, ongoing asset-management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in office conversion is not design but a credit tenant. A hospital is the rare mission-aligned credit with a hard-dollar reason to want housing (turnover cost), and its own back offices are the least visible vacancy on the market.
first_30_days: Build a public-data list of 30 nonprofit systems with admin campuses (IRS Schedule H, county records, satellite parking counts). Cold-pitch a free two-page 'vacancy read' to their real-estate VPs. Convert 2-3 into paid audits within 90 days.

title: PO-Backed Working Capital for Drone Sub-Tier
one_liner: A specialty lender that advances cash against Gauntlet-winner purchase orders to the motor, battery and casting shops that must ship first.
customer: Sub-tier suppliers (motors, ESCs, battery packs, castings, machined parts) with 10-200 staff feeding Drone Dominance winners and Navy autonomy programs; funded by a debt fund or family office.
problem: Insiders think mega-rounds fix the defense supply chain. The AIA-Bain study says no fit-for-purpose investment model exists for sub-tier makers. About 60,000 drones are being ordered, but the people who make the parts are too small for VC and too risky for banks.
solution: Underwrite the prime's award notice and delivery schedule, not the supplier's balance sheet. Offer PO advances, tooling leases and milestone-linked draws, with payment routed through the prime so the loan is self-liquidating. Public award data plus supplier-network mapping is the underwriting edge.
why_now: Gauntlet 2 (Sept 2026) produced roughly 60,000 units of orders. The Navy is stepping back to Series D-F co-investment. $14.6B of 2026 VC is going to primes, not the parts makers beneath them.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% per month on advances (10-15% blended yield), plus origination fees, plus small equity warrants on the best suppliers.
non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not capital in general but capital shaped like a receivable from a credit-worthy prime. Whoever routes payment through the prime turns a scary startup-supplier loan into near-prime credit.
first_30_days: Sign one debt-fund partner for a $5M pilot line. Pull award notices for the 19 Gauntlet 2 firms and cold-call their top 5 suppliers each. Fund 3 small POs against prime payment-assignment letters.

title: Organized Play in a Box for New Card Games
one_liner: A managed service that gives new and crowdfunded trading card games tournament software, judge training, local-game-store onboarding and prize logistics.
customer: New TCG publishers with funded campaigns (for example the Cyberpunk TCG, which raised $28.35M on Kickstarter in April 2026), and their distributors.
problem: Pokemon has sold 85B+ cards, and new TCGs live or die by weekly events at local game stores. First-time creators have big print-run budgets but no rules-aware tournament engine, judge program, store network or prize support. Kickstarter success does not equal retention.
solution: Rules-aware tournament software (decklist validation, banlist updates, Swiss pairing), a certified judge program, store onboarding kits (demo decks, promos, shipping), an event calendar and reporting, and results-integrity tooling.
why_now: The TCG boom and $28M crowdfunding raises create a wave of well-funded first-time publishers. Stores will only stock games with events.
revenue_model: $5-25k per month retainer per game plus $10-30 per event and margin on store kits.
non_obvious_insight: Kickstarter funds the print run, but retention is in weekly events, and store owners only back games that have them. The infrastructure is game-agnostic, so it amortizes across many small TCGs.
first_30_days: Pitch 20 creators of funded TCG campaigns above $250k. Run a pilot kit at 20 stores. Assemble an open-source tournament engine and sell the first two retainers.

title: Human Trust-Anchor Service for Driverless Freight Hubs
one_liner: A neutral crew and signature service at autonomous-truck terminals that replaces the driver's role as freight's witness: pre-trip inspection, condition-of-freight capture, signed digital BOL and inspector liaison, priced per handoff.
customer: Autonomous trucking carriers, the shippers, 3PLs and brokers tendering freight to them, and cargo insurers. The first buyer is a claims-sensitive shipper or a broker like Werner's CIO who says 'we have a gap'.
problem: The driver signs the BOL, counts pieces, notes damage, checks the seal and talks to the inspector. Driverless trucks remove that witness. The CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and requires a trained inspector. PrePass/Kodiak bypass covers 581 sites but is live only in Texas and Louisiana. Paper BOLs delay cash about 60 days and cause six-figure invoice disputes. Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff. Insurers price AV trucks above human ones purely on the unknown.
solution: A per-departure witness desk at transfer hubs and terminals, staffed by trained ex-drivers and ex-inspectors with capture tools. It runs the pre-trip enhanced-inspection checklist and logs the 24-hour clearance. It captures condition of freight (piece count, seal number, photos, weight, temperature, damage detection) and issues a neutral third-party-signed eBOL that shipper, carrier and insurer accept. It also acts as the roadside and first-responder liaison, and packages claims evidence.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and targets 30,000 by 2030. Gatik reports 85k driverless orders. California's driverless-truck rules took effect Apr 28, 2026 and the Teamsters sued on Aug 5. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on Jul 8, 2026. Insurers expect AV truck pricing to fall 15-25% a year, so evidence of loads and conditions moves pricing.
revenue_model: $35-$90 per handoff or departure, well under the current human transfer cost. $4k-$8k/mo per hub as a base fee. Insurer-paid discounts and data license. Claims-evidence packages at $150-$400 per incident.
non_obvious_insight: Driverless trucking is sold as removing labor, but what it actually removes is a witness, and freight claims, inspections and insurance pricing all ran on that witness. Whoever re-supplies trusted witness capacity at transfer hubs becomes a required, neutral node. Because the same crew and signature service serve every AV carrier, no competing carrier will build it.
first_30_days: Pick one Texas corridor and one terminal. Recruit 2-3 ex-inspectors or ex-drivers. Offer a shipper's claims team or a broker a free pilot on 20 AV loads, then $60 per handoff. Sign a cargo insurer as design partner to co-develop the claims-evidence package.

title: Caring Contacts as a Service for Hospitals
one_liner: Outsourced, human-edited follow-up messages and calls after a suicide-risk emergency visit or crisis call, run on a compliance-grade platform hospitals and 988 centers can buy per patient.
customer: Hospital EDs and behavioral units, state-funded 988 crisis centers, university counseling centers and behavioral-health carve-out plans, paying $40-120 per patient enrolled or $5-15k a month per site.
problem: The highest-risk window is the weeks after discharge or a crisis call. The Joint Commission's NPSG 15.01.01 requires follow-up policy, and randomized trials of brief, non-demanding 'caring contact' messages show fewer attempts. Yet most systems run this through one overwhelmed staffer mailing postcards, with no delivery guarantee, tracking or outcome reporting.
solution: A managed service: enrollment at discharge on a tablet, a cadence built from an evidence-based message library (days 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 and beyond), AI drafting with human review, two-way replies routed to trained staff, escalation with warm handoff to crisis lines, and EHR-connected dashboards for Joint Commission and Zero Suicide reporting.
why_now: 988 volume has grown since 2022, about a dozen states now levy 988 telecom fees that fund local centers, and the Harvard study estimating 4,400 fewer youth and young-adult suicide deaths in 988's first 2.5 years strengthens the funding case. 988 politics (Press 3 ended Jul 2025, a restored version excluding Trevor Project announced Jun 2026) push centers toward reliable, defensible operations.
revenue_model: Per-enrollee fee plus platform fee, funded by hospital quality budgets, state 988 funds and SAMHSA grants.
non_obvious_insight: The market chases AI that detects risk, but the best-evidenced and cheapest intervention is a human-sent, non-demanding note. The product is operations and proof (reliable delivery, documentation, outcome reporting), not detection.
first_30_days: Partner with one county crisis center and one hospital ED. Write the message library with a clinical advisor who knows the caring-contacts literature. Enroll 100 patients on a $10k pilot and measure re-contact and re-presentation rates.

title: Certification-Ready OS for Sober Living Operators
one_liner: Software and audit-readiness for independent recovery residences, so the good operators become visible, certified and eligible for opioid-settlement and referral funding.
customer: Independent sober living and recovery residence operators (8-40 beds), who pay a monthly subscription. Counties, states and treatment programs later pay for verified-quality dashboards.
problem: Sober living is a largely informal industry with a few notorious bad actors. States are moving to certification, and funding streams increasingly require it. Good small operators run on spreadsheets and can't prove house rules, incident handling, naloxone logs, drug-testing policies and fair-housing compliance. Funders and hospital discharge planners can't tell who is real.
solution: A recovery-residence operating system built around the NARR standard and each state's certification rules. It covers rent and bed management, house-rule acknowledgments, incident and naloxone logs, drug-test policy records, complaint handling and resident outcomes. It has a gap assessment and mock certification audit, and generates an audit binder. A separate funder dashboard reports verified occupancy and quality metrics.
why_now: Ohio made certification mandatory in January 2025, and Virginia followed in July 2025. New York launched its first recovery residence certification program in early 2025. Certification has become a gatekeeper for state opioid-response subawards, opioid-settlement contracts and Medicaid reimbursement in some states. The SUPPORT reauthorization signed December 1, 2025 extended HUD's Recovery Housing Program and SAMHSA grants through FY2030.
revenue_model: $199-499 per house per month for the operating system. $1,500-3,000 certification-prep packages. Annual license fees from counties, health plans or opioid-settlement administrators for verified-bed and quality dashboards. Do not take pay-per-referral fees: federal and state patient-brokering laws (such as EKRA) make that dangerous.
non_obvious_insight: The gray market's problem is invisibility as much as bad operators: funders have no cheap way to tell good houses from bad. The trusted data trail is the product. The business model rule is to sell software to operators and dashboards to funders, and never take referral commissions. That keeps the network legally clean and trusted by courts, hospitals and families, which is what makes it hard to copy.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a new certification mandate (Ohio or Virginia). Offer 10 operators a free gap assessment against the NARR standard through state recovery-housing associations. Convert them to a $199/month readiness plan. Meet the state certifying body to align templates. Pitch one county opioid-settlement administrator on a pilot verified-bed dashboard.

title: Licensing Workbench for Smallsat Operators
one_liner: A structured software system of record for satellite licensing across spectrum, debris, remote sensing and export control.
customer: Smallsat startups, university missions and new sovereign programs that currently pay law firms and consultants $50-300k per licensing cycle.
problem: Launches and deployments are at record levels (4,517 satellites in 2025), and licensing throughput is the hidden bottleneck. Operators juggle FCC, ITU, NOAA remote-sensing, debris-mitigation and export-control filings. Rules are changing (reported FCC rewrite, the 5-year deorbit rule, the proposed EU Space Act).
solution: A workbench with deterministic calculators (debris assessment, collision probability), templated filings, an ITU coordination tracker, deadline management and an insurer-ready data pack. Add a marketplace to hire specialist counsel. It is not a thin AI wrapper: the value is the structured filing data model and up-to-date rules.
why_now: The 2025-26 regulatory changes and a growing flood of new operators. The EU Space Act, FCC modernization and stricter debris rules all raise the compliance load.
revenue_model: $1-3k per month per mission. Per-filing fees. Referral fees from counsel and consultants.
non_obvious_insight: Every launch boom makes regulatory throughput the binding constraint. The company that owns the data model of a filing becomes the system of record.
first_30_days: Interview 15 smallsat licensing leads about their last filing. Build one calculator plus a deadline tracker for a specific filing, for example an FCC debris assessment. Sign five paying pilots at $500-1,000 per month.

title: Rate-Leak Evidence Packs for Independent Hotels
one_liner: Mystery-shopping plus payout reconciliation that proves when OTA and reseller channels sold below the rate a hotel loaded, packaged as evidence for claims and regulator complaints.
customer: Independent hotels of 20-200 rooms in the EU, UK and US that rely on OTA merchant-model bookings, and hotel associations. The second buyer is a law firm or litigation funder that needs evidence to build a case.
problem: 51% of European hotels say OTAs sell below their loaded rate (up from 40% two years ago), Booking.com handles 66.1% of OTA bookings at surveyed hotels, and 26% of hotels do not know whether rates are passed on. A hotel loads $200, the guest sees $180, and the hotel is paid after checkout. Markups by Agoda, Citi, AA and Southwest loyalty portals are invisible to rate-shopping tools. The only party able to audit the markup is the one being audited.
solution: A panel of real-guest shoppers and reseller-portal quotes covers the hotel's next 90 dates. The results are reconciled against the hotel's folios and payout statements into a 'leak ledger' (date, channel, price shown vs loaded, payout). Timestamped, tamper-evident captures go into a monthly report and an evidence pack the hotel can hand to counsel, an association, a regulator (the EU DMA parity ban) or a claims funder.
why_now: The DMA (Booking designated a gatekeeper in 2024) bans parity clauses, so hotels have new legal options but no proof. The merchant model keeps growing. Fuel and energy shocks (Hormuz, March 2026) and a K-shaped market squeeze lower-tier independents, so recoveries matter.
revenue_model: About EUR 149 per property per month, plus a 20% contingent share of any recovery through a partner law firm or funder. Anonymized leak indices are sold to associations.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence does not exist until someone captures it in real time, and it is perishable because prices change hourly. The firm holding a year of timestamped leaks holds the case file, and OTA self-reporting can never be independent.
first_30_days: Partner with one regional hotel association (Spain, Italy or Croatia). Run a manual 30-date shop of Booking, Expedia, Agoda and two loyalty portals for 20 hotels, and deliver a one-page 'leak map'. Sell a one-off audit at EUR 300, convert 3-5 hotels to the subscription, and take the pack to one litigation funder as proof of concept.

title: Night Season: After-Dark Programming for Heat-Struck Venues
one_liner: A turnkey production company that converts heat-crushed summer attendance at zoos, gardens and ballparks into ticketed after-dark shows, with heat-triggered scheduling, on revenue share.
customer: Zoos, botanical gardens, minor-league ballparks, county fairs and water parks in the Sun Belt and Southwest, whose summer midday attendance collapses in heat waves and who set 2027 programming budgets in Q4.
problem: Extreme heat kills midday visits and creates heat-illness liability, while venue infrastructure sits idle. Venues know night events work (winter light shows, adult zoo nights) but lack lantern, projection or lighting capex, production talent and a heat protocol. New heat rules for outdoor workers in California, Washington and Oregon, with a federal OSHA rule targeted for October 2027, also make midday staffing costlier.
solution: A 'Night Season' program run from June to September. Lantern trails, projection mapping, night-safari tours, film and music nights, with hours moved by a WBGT trigger and a documented heat-safety protocol. We supply the show kit (leased), lighting crew, ticketing setup and sponsors such as hospitals and utilities as 'heat-safe' partners. The venue supplies land and staff.
why_now: Summer 2026 was reported as the hottest US July on record, so 2027 budgets will assume it repeats. LED lantern and projection costs have fallen, and WBGT sensors are cheap. Entertainment production talent is underemployed after studio and game cuts. Venues want revenue that does not depend on midday gates.
revenue_model: 35-45% of ticket and F&B revenue with no fee to the venue, leased show kits, and sponsorships. Illustrative math: 40 nights x 1,000 guests x $22 is about $880K gross per venue-season.
non_obvious_insight: Heat does not kill demand for outdoor leisure. It moves it about eight hours later. What blocks venues is show capex and know-how. A documented WBGT-triggered schedule shift is also a heat-illness risk reduction that a venue's liability insurer may recognize, so the program can help offset its own cost.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 Sun Belt zoos and gardens during the Q4 planning window with a mock-up and a $99 founders-pass landing page at two venues to test pre-sales. Sign a lantern or projection vendor on revenue share. Run a small heat-shifted pilot weekend in Arizona this October, while evenings are warm.

title: Roof Reserve for the ACV Roof Coverage Gap
one_liner: A monthly plan that pre-funds a fixed-price roof replacement, covering the depreciation gap created when owners move to ACV roof coverage.
customer: Homeowners with roofs over 10-12 years old in hail and wildfire states (CO, TX, CA), sold through independent agents and roofers.
problem: Fannie and Freddie (LL-2026-03, Mar 18 2026) now accept actual-cash-value roof coverage. Carriers can cut premiums by moving old roofs to ACV, but the depreciation gap lands on the owner at claim time, often $20-40K. Nobody sells the gap. Hail drives 26-54% of Colorado premiums, so this happens often.
solution: 'Roof Reserve': a $40-90/month prepaid service plan that locks a fixed-price Class 4 or wildfire-rated roof replacement with a vetted roofer and funds the ACV gap after a covered claim. It is structured as a prepaid home-service contract, not insurance (check state rules). Agents earn commission, and the ACV option becomes easier to sell.
why_now: The GSE rule change came in March 2026, and reinsurance softening lets carriers offer ACV options. Colorado now credits documented mitigation.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription plus float, and a 3-6% referral or pre-sold job margin from roofers.
non_obvious_insight: When a regulator loosens a rule to lower premiums, the risk does not disappear. It moves onto the owner's balance sheet, and roofers value a pre-funded pipeline.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 Colorado agencies and 1 roofer. Sell 30 plans to owners whose 12-plus-year roofs are being moved to ACV at renewal. Get a legal read on service-contract versus insurance classification first.

title: Decoy Employees: Canary Tokens for People
one_liner: AI-run fake accounts-payable and help-desk staffers listed where attackers scrape, with voice agents that answer, harvest attacker infrastructure and alert the real team the moment anyone probes.
customer: Security teams at mid-market and enterprise companies in finance, healthcare and professional services, MSPs, and cyber insurers.
problem: Social-engineering crews research org charts and websites to find AP staff and help-desk numbers. Voice-deepfake defenses react only after the call, and defenders get no early warning that they are being targeted. Reports of successful voice-deepfake attacks are rising fast.
solution: Create decoy personas (an AP specialist, a help-desk line) that appear in the company's staff page, vendor portals and public contact lists, never on fake LinkedIn accounts. Each has a mailbox and a monitored voice agent that engages callers safely with no connection to real systems. Every contact triggers an alert with caller number, script, requested bank changes and voice samples, feeds the SIEM, and builds a weekly attack-tempo report for insurers.
why_now: Voice cloning and real-time voice agents make plausible fake clerks cheap. Vishing has surged and attackers automate reconnaissance, so deception is one of the few defenses that scales with attacker automation.
revenue_model: $1.5-3K per month per decoy set, MSP resale, and insurer partnerships.
non_obvious_insight: Canary tokens for files and credentials are standard, but canary employees are not. Decoys turn the attacker's reconnaissance into your telemetry, so the more the attacker automates, the more signal you get.
first_30_days: Build one persona pack with a voice agent and alerting. Deploy at 5 friendly companies with legal and HR sign-off, collect 30 days of hits as proof, and price a $1K per month pilot.

title: Vendor-Neutral ELD Log Auditor and DataQs Filer
one_liner: An independent audit that catches the log errors ELD vendors create, and files the FMCSA challenge when they become violations.
customer: Owner-operators and carriers with 1-50 trucks, plus small DOT-compliance consultants who would white-label it. The driver or carrier owner pays.
problem: ELD software errors turn into violations and fines, and vendor support does not fix them. BigRoad reviewers say 'BigRoad could equal BigFines' because it will 'change your duty status randomly on its own'. They also report that it 'automatically switches to driving', that split sleeper 'doesn't work at all', and that a recent update left them unable to sign their logs. A Motive reviewer says 'it tells me I'm two hours into violation yet in the six past days I've driven 41 hours', and another says 'they cannot take off the violations from ELD'. Motive's following-distance alerts also draw complaints: it 'dings you for following too close when cars pass you in the next lane'.
solution: The driver or carrier emails the standard ELD output file, which every FMCSA-registered ELD must be able to produce (49 CFR 395, Appendix A). The system works with any ELD vendor. It rebuilds the duty timeline and flags implausible auto-driving events, unassigned driving, edits without annotations, split-sleeper and personal-conveyance miscalculations, and form-and-manner errors. It sends a weekly 'audit-ready' report before roadside inspections or compliance audits. When a violation is cited, it assembles a DataQs challenge packet (FMCSA's data-correction request) with the log evidence, GPS or fuel-card timestamps and vendor error messages, ready for the carrier to file.
why_now: FMCSA's DataQs site says that as of September 18, 2026 the revised requirements for State data reviews are in effect, with the stated aim that 'drivers receive their proper due process'. That change is 10 days old and makes challenging bad violations a more credible use of a carrier's time. ELD vendors are still shipping regressions (BigRoad reviewers describe updates that broke log signing and split sleeper in 2026), so the error volume keeps producing challenge-worthy events.
revenue_model: $9 per truck per month for the weekly audit. $99-$199 per DataQs packet. A white-label plan for DOT consultants at $500/month for up to 100 trucks. Later: a discount referral to an insurer that rewards clean, audited logs.
non_obvious_insight: Drivers cannot tell whether the ELD or the driver is wrong, and the vendor has no incentive to tell them. The federal ELD standard gives an open data pipe, so a third party can check any vendor's logs without a vendor integration, and the answer is more credible because the auditor does not sell ELDs. Evidence: BigRoad ELD app reviews (duty status flips, split sleeper broken, 'BigFines') at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=674704833/sortby=mostrecent/xml. Motive reviews (false violation time, violations the vendor cannot remove, following-distance algorithm complaints) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/gomotive.com. The DataQs process and the Sept 18, 2026 change are on FMCSA's own page at https://dataqs.fmcsa.dot.gov/. Carriers already pay for DataQs help, so the willingness to pay is proven. The new part is vendor-neutral log analysis with a challenge packet ready to file.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: read the ELD output file spec, build a parser using FMCSA's sample files and one test ELD, and write the 8 error checks. Days 10-20: recruit 10 owner-operators from trucker Facebook groups and forums for a free audit of their last 8 days. Days 20-30: show each one the specific errors found, charge for the first DataQs packets, and sign 2-3 DOT consultants for the white-label plan. Get a compliance professional to review the packet format.

title: Court-Ready Satellite Emission Evidence for Litigators
one_liner: Expert-witness-grade reports that use hourly geostationary pollution data to document emission events at large industrial sources.
customer: Environmental plaintiffs' firms, community groups with litigation funders, state attorney general offices, and insurers or investors assessing pollution liability.
problem: As federal enforcement priorities shifted in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), private litigation and state action fill the gap. Those actors need independent, admissible evidence, and most cannot interpret satellite data.
solution: Case-specific 'Emission Event Reports' for large point sources (power plants, refineries, LNG terminals, petrochemical complexes). They combine hourly NO2, SO2 and HCHO enhancements from geostationary sounders (NASA TEMPO in North America, Sentinel-4 in Europe), wind reanalysis and thermal flare data, with documented chain of custody and academic expert witnesses.
why_now: Hourly pollution monitoring from geostationary orbit is new: TEMPO has been operating since 2023-24 and Sentinel-4 launched in 2025. Regulatory retreat drives demand for private evidence.
revenue_model: $15-60k per case report. Retainer for firms with recurring dockets. Expert-testimony fees.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation budgets grow when regulation shrinks. A method that survives a Daubert challenge is a defensible moat, because courts reward the first tested method.
first_30_days: Partner with an atmospheric scientist willing to serve as expert. Build a report template on three well-known refinery or power-plant events. Present to five environmental plaintiffs' firms and one state AG office, and sign a first paid case.

title: Turn Foreman Paper Sign-In Sheets Into Court-Ready Records
one_liner: Foremen text a photo of the daily paper sign-in sheet, and the system timestamps it, flags overtime, break and travel-time errors, and builds an audit-ready record. The crew changes nothing.
customer: Trade subcontractors with 5 to 50 field employees (electrical, framing, concrete, HVAC, roofing) that still use paper sheets or Excel. It is sold through construction-focused insurance agents, payroll providers and construction CPAs.
problem: Most contractor wage-hour violations are recordkeeping failures: overtime miscalculations, uncompensated travel time and undocumented breaks. Paper sheets and foreman memory have no audit trail, so when a wage claim lands up to two years later the employer cannot prove what it paid. A $50,000 overtime dispute can double with liquidated damages before attorney fees. Owners don't buy time-tracking software for compliance, because compliance is not what they think they are buying.
solution: A phone number or WhatsApp thread. The foreman photographs the day's sign-in sheet, and the service extracts hours per worker, adds a trusted timestamp, and stores the original image in an append-only log with a chain-of-custody hash. Each week it reconciles hours against the payroll export (CSV from ADP, Gusto or QuickBooks Payroll) and flags mismatches: overtime not paid, drive time between sites, missing breaks, and prevailing-wage or certified-payroll classification gaps. When a claim or audit arrives, one click produces a records package with an affidavit-ready custodian statement. Insurance partners can offer it as a loss-control benefit on wage-and-hour or EPLI coverage.
why_now: Construction Dive ran this as a July 2026 compliance story. DOL Wage and Hour recovered more than $259 million in back wages for nearly 177,000 workers in fiscal 2025, and construction alone saw about 3,000 investigations and $36 million recovered for 21,000 workers. The labor squeeze, with job openings rising for a third month, keeps overtime and crew-hopping high. Photo capture, OCR and trusted timestamping are now cheap enough to deliver this for about $100 a month.
revenue_model: $99 to $299 per month per contractor by headcount; a $750 audit-response records package; a 15 to 20% recurring rebate to insurance agents or payroll partners who resell. Later add payroll-error recovery reports as a paid add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Apps like time clocks fail because crews resist changing habits, and buyers don't feel compliance risk. So sell defensibility on top of the existing paper behavior instead of replacing it. Evidence: a survey of 180 mid-market contractors found only 4% cited compliance as a concern with time tracking, and 72% who tracked time on paper or spreadsheets 'never raised a compliance concern once in the conversation'. The article notes the records 'can't answer the question' when disputes arise two years later, and cites $259M in DOL back wages and $36M recovered from construction in a single year (https://www.constructiondive.com/news/inaccurate-time-records-contractor-compliance-liability/825438/). The same Construction Dive labor page shows the squeeze (https://www.constructiondive.com/topic/labor/).
first_30_days: Week 1: recruit 5 contractors via a construction CPA or insurance agent friend, and build the intake as a shared phone number plus a spreadsheet and an OCR script. Weeks 2 to 3: run their real sign-in sheets through it, deliver a weekly variance report, and show each owner one specific overtime or drive-time gap. Week 4: charge $149 per month, and present the results to two construction insurance agencies as a loss-control add-on. Target: 8 paying contractors and 1 signed agency partner.
